extracted.intended_audience: sea-anglers, sportsmen, and naturalists interested in Cornish fishing and birding
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, narrative guidance and tactics for catching bass (sea-angling) around the Land's End / Sennen area, with embedded related advice on weather, tackle, bait, timing, and safety. The chapter mixes how-to tips with first-person examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bait selection and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Try multiple baits (pilchard, squid, ray's liver, spider-crab, sand-eel, cuttle-fish, launce) and vary presentation to tempt bass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recounts repeatedly changing bait: “We changed the bait—tried pilchard, squid, ray’s liver, spider-crab; we varied the length of the line, the weight of the lead… It was of no use. ‘They’re not on the feed, sir,’ said old Matthey.” Later he uses cuttle-fish and a sand-eel with success. Practical point: persistently vary baits to match fish appetite and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackle fineness vs. strength selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose line and cast appropriate to water clarity and the size/behavior of bass (single salmon-gut, sea-trout cast, rod length and strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes using single salmon-gut initially, then resolving “to substitute a sea-trout cast,” and using a sixteen-foot salmon-rod. He balances fineness (to avoid alarming fish) against strength (to avoid breakage when a monster runs). Example: gut snapped once, so stronger/appropriate tackle matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish according to water clarity and feed behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Bass behavior changes with water clarity and feed: clear water makes them wary; thick or stirred water can improve chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: in clear water bass are very difficult to capture—‘no fish is more difficult to capture in clear water than the bass.’ Conversely, Matthey said ‘What’s wanted… is a bit of a tumble, to stir the bottom and thicken the water.’ Advice: adjust tactics by water condition—when water is thickened or on a spate fish may feed more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe weather and sea signs for timing and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch barometer, seabird behavior, and sky for premonitory tokens of storm and to time fishing outings safely and productively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: ‘a weather-dog was seen… which made the older fishermen shake their heads’ and ‘the glass had fallen to storm-level and the seabirds with wild cries were making for the southern cliffs.’ Guidance: heed local weather signs to protect boats and pick good fishing windows; safety note—avoid venturing out when sea too rough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move fishing ground when fish shift
rubrics_metrics.description: If bass aren't biting in one spot, vary location—try tidal races, headlands, points, and different stretches of coast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author tried Longships, Cowloe rocks, Roarer Point, three miles between Land’s End and Porthgwarra, and more. Recommendation: be willing to relocate; bass may have ‘shifted their quarters.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time-of-day strategy: dawn and night fishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Target low-light periods (dawn, night) as bass can be more catchable then; night cover can reduce wariness in clear water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: ‘the next best time to the grey of early dawn—an hour which has no great charm for me—to fish under cover of night.’ He returns at night, waits until high water and darkness, and succeeds with a large bass. Practical tip: use darkness to overcome fish wariness in clear water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealth, concealment, and unobtrusive presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid alarming fish by moving cautiously, crouching, holding line loosely, and presenting the bait naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the angler ‘crouch[ed], lest he should catch sight of me,’ held the line ‘loosely between my nervous fingers for fear of alarming them,’ and allowed bait to sink then drew it to pass within a foot of a bass’s nose. Advice: stealth and subtle presentation can persuade suspicious bass to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing the strike and patient observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wait for clear signs (tug, drawing of slack) before setting the hook; do not strike prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: a ‘slight tug at the line… followed by the drawing of the slack through my fingers’ preceded the strike. The author stresses attentive, patient handling—‘I had jumped to my feet on feeling the fish… and drove the hook home.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Rod technique and playing a big fish
rubrics_metrics.description: Use steady, controlled leverage (bring the point back over the shoulder, apply steady strain) and work the fish to exhaustion rather than jerking; be mindful of gear limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes grasping the rod and line, bringing the point back over his shoulder slowly to avoid a jerk, applying all the strain he dared, and using the top joint to help tire the fish. Practical guidance: combine rod technique and body position to avoid snap or loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate methods: spinning, hand-line, and spinning-flight
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the method suited to situation: spinning flights, hand-line, or rod-casting depending on location, depth, and target behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text references using a spinning-flight and launce on the rod, a hand-line with sand-eel, and trailing baits near schools. Choose the method that gives correct presentation and control in that spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation: sink-and-draw, and close passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Present bait to pass very close to the fish (within a foot) and vary sink/retrieve (allow sink then draw rapidly) to imitate prey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author’s tactic: ‘allowing it to sink, drew it rapidly through the water so that it passed within a foot of his nose.’ He also notes the spin of the silvery bait being irresistible when properly presented. Emphasizes lure action and proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local knowledge, proverbs, and experienced advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Heed local fishermen’s experience and folk wisdom about where and when fish bite (e.g., ‘When the corn is in the shock, The fish is on the rock’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mate Matthey provides practical counsel about water conditions and spots. The author quotes Cornish proverb and accepts local guidance—use local expertise to inform tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety around shore and rock-fishing hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of run-ins, treacherous currents, quicksand, and risk from breakers when fishing from shore or rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings in text: ‘that treacherous run in the water which from time to time costs the life of a rock-fisher,’ and the author himself nearly swept off his feet in the breakers and had to extricate his legs from quicksand. Advice: maintain safe distance, understand local hazards, and avoid risky positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read wildlife (birds, seals, etc.) as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe seabird and other wildlife movements to locate feeding schools and anticipate sea conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes seabirds making for southern cliffs before storm and earlier describes watching schools of bass by their play at the surface. Using wildlife behavior as a cue can help find feeding fish or warn of weather changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reloading, preparedness, and equipment limitations for shooting
rubrics_metrics.description: For game shooting, account for weapon limitations (muzzle-loader reloading time) and be prepared so as not to miss easy shots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hunting vignette: both barrels were empty when a second woodcock rose—‘the reloading of a muzzle-loader takes time’—leading to a missed shot. Practical rule: anticipate reloading needs and manage gun readiness in fast birdwork.
